title: An Honest Conversation with Bobby Lee & Oliver Tree
summary: A heavily edited three-person film about performance, artistic influence, recovery, resentment and attempted repair. Oliver Tree describes The Choe Show as a formative model for large-scale art and explains his mask as protection from praise and hatred. Bobby Lee and David Choe move from comic performance into a conflict about treatment, sobriety, one-upmanship and friendship, then exchange apologies and affection. The source repeatedly mixes staged bits, music, reenactment, physical exercises and candid disclosure. The editorial layer preserves every idea and direct boundary while refusing to turn the edit into a continuous literal conversation or to publish unvalidated named turns.

connections.why: Choe again frames fear as something to move through, but the episode immediately tests why consent and a hard timeout remain separate from that philosophy.
Found wood and broken doors connect material scarcity to the later ambition for funded large-scale environments.
A prior body-painting memory produces an unambiguous present refusal and a concrete harm account.
The cast directly questions whether contact exists outside recorded performance.
The exercise cannot be summarized as freeing without the audible pain and stop evidence.
The A.A. Promises are recited, interrupted and altered, joining recovery text to interpretive performance.
The episode repeatedly asks whether admiration is honest, performed, demanded or protective.
Oliver returns to the parent-room encounter as a model of participation and emotional risk.
The forced compliment exposes the contradiction between wanting recognition and distrusting praise.
Oliver explicitly distinguishes his public character from private self, a crucial archive-wide warning against reading performance literally.
The Choe Show becomes evidence of what funding, collaborators and an institutional army can enable.
The familiar early-art story appears again, but a damaged price line must not be repaired from memory.
A twenty-year sobriety claim is followed by relapse and a time-bounded thirty-day status; none should be published alone.
David Chang is invoked as a parallel for how years-in-treatment comparisons can turn shared recovery language into hierarchy.

source_notes.claim: The performed passage is the A.A. 'Promises.'
source_notes.assessment: A.A.'s official explanation locates the passage in Chapter 6 of the Big Book. The source performance omits lines and inserts direct-address insults, so it is not a clean reading.

source_notes.claim: Oliver says he was finishing art school at CalArts.
source_notes.assessment: CalArts is the institution named in the recording. The archive should preserve this as Oliver's autobiographical account rather than infer a degree or date from the clip alone.

source_notes.claim: The cast discusses EMDR in treatment.
source_notes.assessment: EMDR is a clinician-led psychotherapy; the clip establishes only that a participant reports undergoing it, not a diagnosis, protocol or outcome.

speaker_policy.reason: The video makes participant identity visually inferable in many scenes, but the transcript is cut across music, reenactment, overlapping speech and montage. No listening-verified turn boundaries or held-out acoustic identity windows exist for this item. Names may index the work; line-level speaker labels remain withheld.
